questions.prompt: The squared residual \(\lVert Ax-b\rVert^2\) has gradient \(2A^T(Ax-b)\). Ridge adds \(\lambda\lVert x\rVert^2\) with \(\lambda > 0\). Setting the full gradient to zero gives
options: \((A^T A+\lambda I)x = A^T b\)
\((A^T A)x = A^T b+\lambda x\)
\((A+\lambda I)x = b\)
\(A^T A x = \lambda A^T b\)
questions.explanation: The penalty \(\lambda\lVert x\rVert^2\) contributes \(2\lambda x\) to the gradient. Moving that term to the left adds \(\lambda I\) to \(A^T A\). Leaving \(\lambda x\) on the right of the unshifted normal equation hides the unknown \(x\). Adding \(\lambda I\) to \(A\) is not the gradient of the penalty. Scaling only the right-hand side by \(\lambda\) is a different objective.

questions.prompt: One coefficient, two observations: the column of \(A\) is \((1,1)\), \(b = (3,1)\), and \(\lambda = 2\). What is the ridge solution?
questions.explanation: \(A^T A = 2\) and \(A^T b = 4\). The shifted equation is \((2+2)x = 4\), so \(x = 1\). Ordinary least squares would divide 4 by 2 and give 2. Dividing by \(\lambda\) alone gives \(4/2 = 2\) as well, and it drops the Gram entry. The mean of the observations is 2, which is not the coefficient.

questions.prompt: Positive definite matrices are the ones whose eigenvalues are positive. For \(\lambda > 0\), the ridge matrix \(A^T A+\lambda I\) is
options: positive definite only when \(A\) already has independent columns
positive definite whether or not the columns of \(A\) are independent
singular whenever \(A\) is singular
indefinite, because \(\lambda I\) subtracts from the eigenvalues
questions.explanation: Every eigenvalue of \(A^T A\) is at least 0, and adding \(\lambda > 0\) makes every eigenvalue at least \(\lambda\). Independent columns are not required. A singular \(A\) makes \(A^T A\) singular, but the shift removes that singularity. The shift adds, so it does not make the form indefinite.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that solves a ridge problem with penalty weight lambda.
questions.explanation: The shift is applied to the Gram matrix, so the Gram matrix comes first. The solve uses the shifted matrix, so it comes after the addition. Adding \(\lambda\) to \(A\) before forming \(A^T A\) is a different algorithm and is not these steps. Solving the unshifted system first produces ordinary least squares, not the system written in the last step.

steps: Form the Gram matrix A^T A and the vector A^T b.
Add lambda to each diagonal entry of that Gram matrix.
Solve the shifted linear system for x.

questions.prompt: Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(b = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\), and \(\lambda = 1\). What is the second coordinate of the ridge solution?
questions.explanation: \(A^T A = \mathrm{diag}(2,1)\) and \(A^T b = (4,2)\). After the shift, the second equation is \((1+1)x_2 = 2\), so \(x_2 = 1\). Ordinary least squares would leave the second diagonal entry at 1 and give \(x_2 = 2\). The first ridge coordinate is \(4/3\), not the second. The observation 2 is the third entry of \(b\), and it is also the second entry of \(A^T b\). The shift leaves that entry alone and changes the diagonal, so the solution's second coordinate is \(2/2 = 1\), not the entry 2 itself.

questions.prompt: For the same \(A\), \(b\), and \(\lambda = 1\), what is the first coordinate of the ridge solution?
questions.explanation: The shifted first equation is \((2+1)x_1 = 4\), so \(x_1 = 4/3\). Ordinary least squares divides 4 by 2 and gives 2. The second ridge coordinate is 1. The sum of the two ridge coordinates is \(7/3\), which is not the first coordinate.

questions.prompt: Let \(t > 0\) and \(\mathrm{lam} > 0\). The column of \(A\) is \((t,t)\), the right-hand side is \((t,0)\), and the penalty weight is lam. Write the ridge solution as an expression in t and lam.
questions.explanation:
\(A^T A = 2t^2\) and \(A^T b = t^2\). The shifted scalar equation is \((2t^2+\mathrm{lam})x = t^2\).
• \(t^2/(2t^2)\) is ordinary least squares, with the penalty left out.
• \(t/(2t+\mathrm{lam})\) cancels only one factor of \(t\) and is a different function.
• \(\mathrm{lam}/(2t^2)\) inverts the roles of the Gram entry and the penalty.

questions.prompt: Which statements match the penalty \(\lVert Ax-b\rVert^2+\lVert\Gamma x\rVert^2\)?
options: The stationarity equation is \((A^T A+\Gamma^T\Gamma)x = A^T b\).
Ridge is the case \(\Gamma = \sqrt{\lambda}\, I\).
The shift \(\Gamma^T\Gamma\) can be any symmetric positive semidefinite matrix of that form.
The penalty \(\lVert\Gamma x\rVert^2\) is the same term as \(\lambda\lVert x\rVert_1\).
questions.explanation: The gradient of \(\lVert\Gamma x\rVert^2\) contributes \(2\Gamma^T\Gamma x\), so the normal matrix gains \(\Gamma^T\Gamma\). Choosing \(\Gamma = \sqrt{\lambda}\, I\) recovers \(\lambda I\). Any Gram matrix \(\Gamma^T\Gamma\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite. The absolute penalty \(\lambda\lVert x\rVert_1\) is a different function, and its stationarity condition is not this linear shift.

questions.prompt: Compared with ordinary least squares, a ridge solution with \(\lambda > 0\)
options: always has a larger Euclidean norm, because the penalty adds a positive term
is unchanged, because the normal equations already have a unique solution
cannot be computed unless \(A^T A\) is invertible
has a smaller or equal Euclidean norm, with equality only in degenerate cases such as a zero right-hand side
questions.explanation: The ridge objective charges \(\lambda\lVert x\rVert^2\), so the minimizer does not move farther from the origin than the ordinary minimizer. When the ordinary solution is already zero, both solutions are zero. A positive \(\lambda\) changes a nonzero ordinary solution. The shifted matrix is invertible for \(\lambda > 0\) even when \(A^T A\) is not.

questions.prompt: One step below is false. Select that step, and the reason it fails. Here \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(b = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\), and \(\lambda = 1\).
questions.explanation: The Gram matrix and the shifted diagonal are correct, and the shifted system does solve to \((4/3, 1)\). Ordinary least squares solves \(\mathrm{diag}(2,1)x = (4,2)\) and gets \((2, 2)\), which is a different point. A positive penalty moves a nonzero ordinary solution. The false step is the claim that the minimizer is unchanged.

questions.figure_alt: A 3 by 2 matrix with two copies of the first standard basis row and one copy of the second.
steps: A^T A = diag(2, 1) and A^T b = (4, 2).
Adding lambda on the diagonal produces diag(3, 2).
The ridge minimizer equals the ordinary least-squares minimizer, because a positive lambda does not move the solution.
Solving the shifted system produces x = (4/3, 1).
reasons: Adding lambda I moves the eigenvalues, so the minimizer changes unless the ordinary solution is already zero.
The shift should be added to A before multiplying by A^T, and that is the false step.
The right-hand side should be divided by lambda, so the reported solution is the false step.

questions.prompt: A later absolute penalty is different, but the general squared penalty is still this skill. Take \(A = I\), \(b = (1,3)\), and \(\Gamma = \mathrm{diag}(2,0)\). What is the first coordinate of the minimizer of \(\lVert Ax-b\rVert^2+\lVert\Gamma x\rVert^2\)?
questions.explanation: \(\Gamma^T\Gamma = \mathrm{diag}(4,0)\), so the shifted matrix is \(\mathrm{diag}(5,1)\). The first equation is \(5x_1 = 1\), hence \(x_1 = 1/5\). The second coordinate stays 3, because \(\Gamma\) does not charge it. Ordinary least squares would leave \(x_1 = 1\). Using \(\Gamma\) instead of \(\Gamma^T\Gamma\) would shift the first diagonal by 2 and give \(1/3\).

questions.prompt: A Gaussian prior on the coefficients, with mean zero and covariance proportional to \(I/\lambda\), has a negative log density equal to a constant plus \(\lambda\lVert x\rVert^2\). Maximizing likelihood times that prior is
options: ordinary least squares, because a prior does not change the maximizer
an absolute penalty on \(x\)
the ridge problem with penalty weight \(\lambda\)
a shift added to \(A\) rather than to \(A^T A\)
questions.explanation: The log of a spherical Gaussian prior is a squared Euclidean penalty, up to scaling and an additive constant. Adding it to the squared residual is ridge. An absolute penalty is a different prior, with a Laplacian shape. A prior changes the maximizer whenever \(\lambda > 0\) and the ordinary solution is nonzero. The algebra of the gradient puts the shift on \(A^T A\).
